title: Doubles & Triples
summary: How to drive, couple, uncouple and inspect double and triple trailers, which are less stable than any other rig.

blocks.text: Doubles and triples are less stable than other commercial vehicles, and more things can go wrong. Take special care.

items: Steer gently and go slowly around corners, on-ramps, off-ramps and curves.
A curve speed that is safe for a straight truck or single-trailer rig may be too fast for doubles or triples.

The crack-the-whip effect, caused by rearward amplification, makes them more likely to turn over than other combinations. A quick lane change can flip the last trailer, which is the one most likely to turn over.
Triples have a rearward amplification of about 3.5: the last trailer rolls 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor.
Look far ahead so you can slow down or change lanes gradually. Smooth driving prevents rollovers and jackknifes.

rows: Following distance
1 second per 10 feet of length, plus 1 second above 40 mph. A 70-foot set at 55 mph needs 7 + 1 = 8 seconds.
Gaps
They are longer and can't turn or stop suddenly. Wait for large gaps before entering or crossing traffic, and be sure you're clear at the sides before changing lanes.
Bad weather and mountains
More length and more dead axles for the drive axles to pull mean more chance of skids and lost traction.
Parking
Don't pull into a spot you can't pull straight through. Know the lot layout.

blocks.text: A converter dolly (converter gear) is a coupling device with one or two axles and a fifth wheel. It lets a semitrailer be coupled to the back of a tractor-trailer to make a double.

items: Dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have antilock brakes. You can tell by the yellow ABS lamp on the left side of the dolly.
To release dolly brakes, open the dolly air tank petcock. If it has spring brakes, use the dolly parking brake control.
A dolly or trailer without spring brakes holds only while air remains in its tank. Chock its wheels when parked.

blocks.text: Put the more heavily loaded trailer first, right behind the tractor, and the lighter one in the rear. For example, with 32,000 lb and 18,000 lb trailers, the 18,000-lb trailer goes in back.

items: Secure the rear trailer. If it has no spring brakes, connect the emergency line, charge its tank, then disconnect the line. This sets its emergency brakes (if slack adjusters are right). Chock the wheels if you have any doubt.

Release the dolly brakes and wheel the dolly in front of the second trailer, lined up with its kingpin. (Or tow it into place with the first trailer, locking the pintle hook and raising the dolly support for the move.)
Back the first trailer up to the dolly tongue, hook the dolly to it, lock the pintle hook, and secure the dolly support in the raised position.
Make sure the rear trailer's brakes are locked and/or its wheels chocked.
Check the rear trailer's height. It must be slightly lower than the center of the dolly's fifth wheel, so it rises slightly as the dolly goes under.
Back the dolly under the rear trailer.
Raise the landing gear slightly off the ground so it isn't damaged if the trailer moves.
Test the coupling by pulling against the pin of the second trailer.
Look at the coupling: no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, and the locking jaws closed on the kingpin.
Connect the safety chains, air hoses and light cords.
Close the dolly air tank petcock and the shut-off valves at the rear of the second trailer. Open the shut-offs at the rear of the first trailer (and on the dolly if it has them).
Raise the landing gear completely.
Push in the air supply knob, then open the emergency line shut-off at the rear of the second trailer. If no air comes out, something is wrong and the brakes won't work.
Park the rig in a straight line on firm, level ground and set the parking brakes.
Chock the second trailer's wheels if it has no spring brakes.
Lower the second trailer's landing gear enough to take some weight off the dolly.
Close the air shut-offs at the rear of the first trailer (and on the dolly if equipped). Disconnect and secure the dolly's air and electric lines.
Release the dolly brakes and the dolly fifth wheel latch.
Slowly pull the tractor, first trailer and dolly forward to draw the dolly out from under the rear trailer.
Lower the dolly landing gear, disconnect the safety chains, and set the dolly spring brakes or chock its wheels.
Release the pintle hook on the first trailer and slowly pull clear.

blocks.text: Never unlock the pintle hook while the dolly is still under the rear trailer. The tow bar can fly up, injuring you and making it very hard to re-couple.

items: Triples, coupling: couple the tractor to the first trailer as for any tractor-semitrailer, then add each trailer with a dolly the same way as doubles.
Triples, uncoupling: uncouple the third (last) trailer first by pulling out its dolly and unhitching it, then uncouple the rest like a double.
For less common combinations, follow the manufacturer's and/or owner's instructions.

blocks.text: Use the standard seven-step inspection, plus these extra checks for the coupling system, dollies and shut-off valves.

items: Fifth wheel: securely mounted, greased, no visible gap between upper and lower plates, jaws around the shank (not the head) of the kingpin, safety latch engaged.
Sliding fifth wheel: locked in place, and not so far forward that the tractor frame hits the landing gear or the cab hits the trailer in turns.
Air lines: connected to the glad hands, supported, free of leaks and damage, with enough slack for turns. Light cords firmly in their sockets.
Landing gear: fully raised, undamaged, crank handle in place and secured.
Dolly: pintle eye in the pintle hook, hook latched, safety chains secured, and any spare tire on the dolly secured.

rows: Shut-offs at rear of front trailers (including the middle trailer of triples)
OPEN
Shut-offs at rear of the last trailer
CLOSED
Converter dolly air tank drain valve
CLOSED

blocks.text: Check the brakes as you would on any combination vehicle, plus make sure air reaches every trailer. You must have air all the way to the back for all the brakes to work.

items: Hold the rig with the tractor parking brake and/or wheel chocks, and wait for normal air pressure.
Push in the red trailer air supply knob to charge the emergency (supply) lines. Apply the trailer hand brake to put air in the service line.
At the rear of the last trailer, open the emergency line shut-off and listen for air, then close it.
Open the service line valve and listen for air, then close it. This works only while the hand brake or brake pedal is applied.
No air from either line? Check that all shut-off valves on the trailers and dollies are open.

rows: Tractor protection valve

With the system charged and engine off, fan the brake pedal. The air supply knob should pop out at the maker's setting, usually 20 to 45 psi. If it fails, a trailer leak could drain the tractor's air and set the emergency brakes.
Trailer emergency brakes
Check the trailer rolls freely, then pull out the air supply knob and tug gently. The trailer should hold.
Trailer service brakes
Roll forward slowly and apply the trailer hand valve. You should feel the brakes. In normal driving, control the brakes with the foot pedal.

keyPoints: Doubles and triples are the least stable rigs; steer gently and slow down for curves and ramps.
The last trailer is the most likely to roll over because of the crack-the-whip effect.
Put the heavier trailer first, right behind the tractor.
Leave extra following distance and bigger gaps, and park only where you can pull straight through.
The rear trailer must sit slightly lower than the dolly's fifth wheel before you back under it.
Never unlock the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer.
Shut-offs: open at the rear of front trailers, closed at the rear of the last trailer; dolly drain closed.
Confirm air reaches the back of the last trailer, or the brakes won't work.
